function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m not able to run commands or push to a remote repository from here, but I can walk you through the exact steps you’d need to take on your own machine (or in a CI job) to accomplish what you described.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# SSH clone – make sure you have the key set up for git@github.com
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

If you prefer HTTPS:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

Open the folder and look for:

| File | What to look for |
|------|------------------|
| `package.json` | Entry point (`main`), scripts (`start`, `dev`), dependencies |
| `src/` or `app.js` | Where the server starts, port it listens on |
| `README.md` | Any hints about environment variables or ports |
| `.gitignore` | Common patterns to keep out of the image |

> **Tip** – If the repo contains a `Dockerfile` already, you can either update it or replace it entirely. For a clean start, let’s create a fresh one.

### 2.2 Create a Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root with the following content (adjust the base image and entrypoint as needed):

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on (replace 3000 with your actual port)
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and stable.  
> * `npm ci` ensures reproducible installs.  
> * `EXPOSE 3000` tells Docker which port the container will listen on (adjust if your app uses a different port).  
> * `CMD ["npm", "start"]` runs the script defined in `package.json`.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAML

Create a file called `k8s-deployment.yaml` (or split into `deployment.yaml` and `service.yaml`) with the following template:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your image repo
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000   # adjust if your app uses a different port
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000   # maps service port 80 to container port 3000
```

> **What to replace**  
> * `<YOUR_REGISTRY>` – e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq` or `docker.io/zelarhq`.  
> * `3000` – the port your Node app actually listens on (check `app.js` or `package.json`).  

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: '18'   # match your Docker base image

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test   # only if you have tests

    - name: Build Docker image
      run: |
        docker build -t ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest .
        echo ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} | docker login ghcr.io -u ${{ github.actor }} --password-stdin
        docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
      # Add your deployment step here if you want automatic deployment
```

> **Key points**  
> * Uses the `GITHUB_TOKEN` secret to log in to GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`).  
> * Builds and pushes the image tagged `latest`.  
> * You can extend the workflow to deploy to a cluster if you have a `kubectl` context set up.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s-deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

If you replaced an existing Dockerfile or YAML, you might want to `git rm` the old ones first.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **What happens next?**  
> * The GitHub Actions workflow will trigger on the push, build the image, and push it to GHCR.  
> * If you added a deployment step, it will also apply the manifests to your cluster.

---

### Quick checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|----|------|
| ✅ | `Dockerfile` created/updated |
| ✅ | `k8s-deployment.yaml` created |
| ✅ | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` created |
| ✅ | Files staged (`git add`) |
| ✅ | Commit & push (`git commit && git push`) |

That’s it! Once you’ve pushed, you can verify the workflow run in the **Actions** tab of your GitHub repo, and check that the image appears in **Packages → Container**. If you’re using a Kubernetes cluster, you can run `kubectl get pods -l app=nodejs-welcome` to see the new pods coming up.
